Data Structure Interpretation¶

The dataset contains 4018 daily observations from 2015 to 2025.

No missing values or duplicate rows were found in the original dataset, indicating that the reanalysis data provided a complete and consistent time series for modelling.

Summary Statistics¶

The average daily maximum temperature was approximately 22.23°C, with values ranging from 10.9°C to 37.4°C.

Precipitation was generally low, with a median of 0 mm, indicating many dry days, although the maximum precipitation value of 80.8 mm shows that some days experienced heavy rainfall.

The daily maximum temperature series shows strong short-term fluctuations. The 30-day moving average smooths these daily changes and makes the seasonal pattern easier to observe. The repeated rises and falls over time indicate clear annual seasonality, with warmer and cooler periods recurring across years.

The linear trend provides a general indication of long-term direction, although the dominant pattern in the series appears to be seasonal variation rather than a strong linear trend.

The distribution of daily maximum temperature is centred around approximately 22°C, with most values concentrated between 18°C and 26°C. The mean value of 22.23°C is very close to the median value of 22.05°C, suggesting that the distribution is reasonably balanced. However, the maximum value of 37.4°C indicates the presence of occasional hot days, which may contribute to a slight upper tail in the distribution.

In [259]:
sns.boxplot(x=df["TMAX"])
plt.title("Boxplot of Maximum Temperature")
plt.show()

The boxplot shows that the median daily maximum temperature is approximately 22°C, with the middle 50% of values lying between 18.1°C and 25.6°C. This indicates moderate variability in daily maximum temperature. The upper end of the distribution extends to 37.4°C, which may appear as a high-temperature outlier according to the interquartile range rule. However, such values are physically plausible for hot days and were therefore retained in the analysis rather than treated as data errors.

In [260]:
df_stl = df.set_index("time")

stl = STL(df_stl["TMAX"], period=365)
result = stl.fit()

result.plot()
plt.show()

STL decomposition was used to separate the TMAX time series into trend, seasonal, and residual components. The seasonal component helps confirm recurring annual temperature patterns, while the residual component captures irregular variation not explained by trend or seasonality.

Interpretation:

The observed component shows the original daily maximum temperature series. The series contains strong day-to-day fluctuations, but repeated annual rises and falls are visible, indicating seasonal variation in maximum temperature.

Trend component: The trend component captures the longer-term movement in maximum temperature after the seasonal pattern has been removed. The trend appears smoother than the observed series and suggests gradual variation over time rather than abrupt changes. This indicates that while long-term variation exists, the dominant pattern in the data is seasonal.

Seasonal component: The seasonal component shows a clear repeating annual pattern, confirming that maximum temperature follows a strong seasonal cycle. This supports the inclusion of cyclical time-based features, such as sine and cosine transformations of month and day of year, in the machine learning models

Resisual component: The residual component represents irregular variation that is not explained by the trend or seasonal components. The presence of residual fluctuations suggests that daily maximum temperature contains short-term variability, which supports the use of machine learning models capable of capturing nonlinear and complex relationships.

The data was split chronologically, with the earliest observations used for training, the middle period used for calibration, and the most recent period used for testing. This preserved the temporal order of the data and avoided data leakage.

8. Fit all models and evaluate point predictions¶

In [273]:
point_results = []
trained_models = {}

for name, model in models.items():
    print(f"Training {name}...")
    
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    trained_models[name] = model
    
    y_pred = model.predict(X_test)
    
    mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_pred)
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred))
    r2 = r2_score(y_test, y_pred)
    
    point_results.append({
        "Model": name,
        "MAE": mae,
        "RMSE": rmse,
        "R2": r2
    })

point_results_df = pd.DataFrame(point_results)

8. Apply Conformal Prediction to all three models¶

In [274]:
conformal_results = {}
summary_results = []

confidence_level = 0.90

for name, model in trained_models.items():
    print(f"Applying conformal prediction to {name}...")
    
    cp_model = SplitConformalRegressor(
        estimator=model,
        confidence_level=confidence_level,
        prefit=True
    )
    
    cp_model.conformalize(X_cal, y_cal)
    
    y_pred, intervals = cp_model.predict_interval(X_test)
    
    lower = intervals[:, 0, 0]
    upper = intervals[:, 1, 0]
    
    mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_pred)
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred))
    r2 = r2_score(y_test, y_pred)
    
    coverage = ((y_test >= lower) & (y_test <= upper)).mean()
    avg_width = np.mean(upper - lower)
    
    summary_results.append({
        "Model": name,
        "MAE": mae,
        "RMSE": rmse,
        "R2": r2,
        "Coverage": coverage,
        "Average Interval Width": avg_width
    })
    
    conformal_results[name] = {
        "y_pred": y_pred,
        "lower": lower,
        "upper": upper
    }

results_df = pd.DataFrame(summary_results)
results_df

Before hyperparameter tuning, the MLP model achieved the best predictive performance. It produced the lowest MAE of 2.273°C, the lowest RMSE of 3.074°C, and the highest R² value of 0.660. This indicates that, among the three initial models, MLP made the smallest average prediction errors and explained the largest proportion of variation in next-day maximum temperature.

Random Forest and XGBoost performed similarly in terms of MAE, with values of 2.363°C and 2.361°C, respectively. However, Random Forest had a slightly better RMSE and R² than XGBoost. This suggests that although XGBoost had marginally lower average absolute error, Random Forest handled larger errors slightly better in the untuned setting.

For conformal prediction performance, all three models produced coverage close to the target 90% level. XGBoost achieved the highest coverage at 90.38%, meaning its prediction intervals captured slightly more than the required proportion of actual observations. However, this came with the widest average interval width of 10.586°C. This suggests that XGBoost was more conservative: it achieved higher coverage partly by producing wider intervals. MLP achieved coverage of 90.22% with a slightly narrower interval width than XGBoost. This means that before tuning, MLP offered the best balance between predictive accuracy and uncertainty reliability.

12. Hyperparameter Tuning¶

In [283]:
from sklearn.model_selection import GridSearchCV, TimeSeriesSplit
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.neural_network import MLPRegressor
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from xgboost import XGBRegressor

tscv = TimeSeriesSplit(n_splits=5)

models = {
    "Random Forest": {
        "model": RandomForestRegressor(random_state=42),
        "params": {
            "n_estimators": [100, 300],
            "max_depth": [None, 10, 20],
            "min_samples_leaf": [1, 2]
        }
    },

    "XGBoost": {
        "model": XGBRegressor(
            objective="reg:squarederror",
            random_state=42
        ),
        "params": {
            "n_estimators": [100, 300],
            "learning_rate": [0.05, 0.1],
            "max_depth": [3, 5]
        }
    },

    "MLP": {
        "model": Pipeline([
            ("scaler", StandardScaler()),
            ("mlp", MLPRegressor(
                max_iter=1000,
                random_state=42
            ))
        ]),
        "params": {
            "mlp__hidden_layer_sizes": [(64,), (64, 32)],
            "mlp__activation": ["relu"],
            "mlp__learning_rate_init": [0.001],
            "mlp__alpha": [0.0001, 0.001]
        }
    }
}
In [284]:
best_models = {}
tuning_results = []

for name, item in models.items():
    print(f"Tuning {name}...")

    grid = GridSearchCV(
        estimator=item["model"],
        param_grid=item["params"],
        cv=tscv,
        scoring="neg_mean_absolute_error",
        n_jobs=-1
    )

    grid.fit(X_train, y_train)

    best_models[name] = grid.best_estimator_

    tuning_results.append({
        "Model": name,
        "Best Parameters": grid.best_params_,
        "Best CV MAE": -grid.best_score_
    })

tuning_results_df = pd.DataFrame(tuning_results)
tuning_results_df

Tuning Random Forest...
Tuning XGBoost...
Tuning MLP...
Out[284]:
Model Best Parameters Best CV MAE
0 Random Forest {'max_depth': 10, 'min_samples_leaf': 2, 'n_es... 2.319575
1 XGBoost {'learning_rate': 0.05, 'max_depth': 3, 'n_est... 2.299902
2 MLP {'mlp__activation': 'relu', 'mlp__alpha': 0.00... 2.362260

The tuning process used MAE as the optimisation criterion because MAE is directly interpretable as average temperature error in degrees Celsius. During cross-validation on the training set, XGBoost achieved the lowest CV MAE of 2.300°C, followed by Random Forest with 2.320°C, and MLP with 2.362°C.

This suggests that, during the internal validation stage, XGBoost had the strongest average validation performance. However, cross-validation results are not the final performance results. The final conclusion must be based on how the tuned models perform on the independent test set, especially after conformal prediction is applied.

A key point here is that the model that performs best during cross-validation does not always perform best on the final test period. This can happen because the test period represents a later time block and may contain different seasonal or weather behaviour from the training folds.

Apply Conformal prediction to tuned models¶

In [285]:
results = []
conformal_results = {}

confidence_level = 0.90

for name, model in best_models.items():
    print(f"Applying conformal prediction to {name}...")

    cp_model = SplitConformalRegressor(
        estimator=model,
        confidence_level=confidence_level,
        prefit=True
    )

    cp_model.conformalize(X_cal, y_cal)

    y_pred, intervals = cp_model.predict_interval(X_test)

    lower = intervals[:, 0, 0]
    upper = intervals[:, 1, 0]

    mae = mean_absolute_error(y_test, y_pred)
    rmse = np.sqrt(mean_squared_error(y_test, y_pred))
    r2 = r2_score(y_test, y_pred)

    coverage = ((y_test >= lower) & (y_test <= upper)).mean()
    avg_width = np.mean(upper - lower)

    results.append({
        "Model": name,
        "MAE": mae,
        "RMSE": rmse,
        "R2": r2,
        "Coverage": coverage,
        "Average Interval Width": avg_width
    })

    conformal_results[name] = {
        "Prediction": y_pred,
        "Lower": lower,
        "Upper": upper
    }

tuned_results_df = pd.DataFrame(results)
tuned_results_df

After hyperparameter tuning, all three models improved in terms of interval width, and the predictive performance improved slightly compared with the untuned versions. The tuned MLP model remained the strongest overall performer, with the lowest MAE of 2.268°C, the lowest RMSE of 3.038°C, and the highest R² of 0.667.

This means that the tuned MLP model had the smallest average prediction error and explained approximately 66.7% of the variation in next-day maximum temperature. In practical terms, the model’s predictions were, on average, about 2.27°C away from the observed next-day maximum temperature. The tuned XGBoost model also improved compared with its untuned version, reducing MAE from 2.361°C to 2.313°C and reducing the average interval width from 10.586°C to 9.682°C. However, its RMSE and R² remained weaker than MLP. This suggests that XGBoost improved after tuning but still did not outperform MLP on the final test set.

Random Forest also improved after tuning, with MAE decreasing from 2.363°C to 2.327°C, RMSE decreasing from 3.097°C to 3.069°C, and R² increasing from 0.654 to 0.661. This shows that tuning helped Random Forest, although it still remained behind MLP in overall predictive accuracy.

After tuning, the prediction intervals became narrower, but the empirical coverage also decreased slightly below the target 90% level. This shows a common trade-off in uncertainty quantification: narrower intervals are more efficient, but they may cover slightly fewer true values. The tuned MLP model produced the narrowest interval width of 9.611°C, while maintaining coverage of 88.89%. This is slightly below the nominal 90% target but still very close. The result suggests that MLP produced the sharpest intervals while still providing reasonably reliable uncertainty estimates.

XGBoost had the second narrowest intervals after tuning, with an average width of 9.682°C, but its coverage dropped to 88.39%. This means that although XGBoost became more efficient in terms of interval width, it undercovered slightly more than MLP. Random Forest had the widest tuned intervals among the three models, with an average width of 9.924°C, and coverage of 88.56%. Overall, tuning improved interval efficiency by narrowing the intervals, but this came at the cost of slightly reduced coverage.

Best Performing Model¶

Overall, the tuned MLP model provided the strongest performance among the models evaluated. It achieved the lowest MAE of 2.268°C, the lowest RMSE of 3.038°C, and the highest R² value of 0.667, indicating that it produced the most accurate point forecasts for next-day maximum temperature. It also produced the narrowest average conformal prediction intervals, with an average width of 9.611°C. Although its empirical coverage of 88.89% was slightly below the nominal 90% level, it remained close to the target and represented the best balance between predictive accuracy and interval efficiency. XGBoost achieved strong validation performance during hyperparameter tuning, but it did not outperform MLP on the final test set. Random Forest showed moderate performance and improved after tuning, but remained weaker than MLP overall.

Conformal Prediction Interpretation¶

Split conformal prediction produced prediction intervals with empirical coverage close to the nominal 90% level. Before hyperparameter tuning, XGBoost and MLP slightly exceeded the 90% target, achieving coverage values of 90.38% and 90.22%, respectively. After tuning, interval widths became narrower across all models, but empirical coverage decreased slightly below 90%. This indicates a trade-off between interval efficiency and coverage. The tuned MLP model achieved the narrowest intervals while maintaining coverage close to the target level, suggesting that it provided the most efficient uncertainty estimates among the tuned models. The slight undercoverage may be explained by the time-series nature of the data, where strict exchangeability is difficult to guarantee.
